f(4x + 3y) = f(3x + y) + f(x + 2y)
$$

sentence:
Add the last two: $$
f(3x + y) + f(x + 2y) = 3a x + a y + a x + 2a y = 4a x + 3a y
$$
sentence-category-reason: Performs explicit algebraic addition and simplification of expressions.

sentence: Which matches $ f(4x + 3y) $.

sentence: Let’s define $ f(n) = an $, and suppose this is the **only** solution.

sentence: We will show that **if** $ f $ satisfies the functional equation, then it must be linear.
sentence-category-reason: Announces the goal to prove that any solution must be linear.

sentence: Let’s define a new function $ g(n) = f(n) - an $ for some constant $ a \in \mathbb{Z} $.
sentence-category-reason: Introduces a new auxiliary function g(n); setting up notation.

sentence: We want to choose $ a $ such that $ g $ satisfies the same functional equation **but with zero on the right-hand side**, i.e., $ g(4x + 3y) = g(3x + y) + g(x + 2y) $.
sentence-category-reason: States the plan/goal for choosing a so that g satisfies a targeted equation.

sentence: Let’s try to find such an $ a $.
sentence-category-reason: Declares the intention to determine such a parameter a.

sentence:
Let’s compute both sides using $ f(n) = an + g(n) $: Left-hand side: $$
f(4x + 3y) = a(4x + 3y) + g(4x + 3y)
$$
sentence-category-reason: Computes the left-hand side using the decomposition f = an + g.

sentence:
Right-hand side: $$
f(3x + y) + f(x + 2y) = a(3x + y) + g(3x + y) + a(x + 2y) + g(x + 2y)
$$
sentence-category-reason: Computes the right-hand side using the same decomposition.
Carries out algebraic simplification on the right-hand side.

sentence:
So the equation becomes: $$
a(4x + 3y) + g(4x + 3y) = a(4x + 3y) + g(3x + y) + g(x + 2y)
$$
sentence-category-reason: Presents the derived equation after substitution; continuation of algebraic manipulation.

sentence:
Canceling $ a(4x + 3y) $ from both sides: $$
g(4x + 3y) = g(3x + y) + g(x + 2y)
$$
sentence-category-reason: Cancels common terms to obtain the functional equation for g.

sentence: So $ g $ satisfies the same functional equation.

sentence: We want to show that $ g(n) = 0 $ for all $ n $, which would mean $ f(n) = an $ is the only solution.

We want to show that the **only** integer function $ g: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z} $ satisfying: $$
g(4x + 3y) = g(3x + y) + g(x + 2y)
$$

Let’s use the identities we derived earlier for $ f $, and apply them to $ g $: From earlier: $$
f(3y) = f(y) + f(2y) \Rightarrow g(3y) = g(y) + g(2y)
$$
sentence-category-reason: Applies previously known identities to deduce a relation for g.

sentence: Let’s now suppose $ a \ne 0 $, and try to get a contradiction.

sentence: Then $ g(n) $ is unbounded as $ n \to \infty $, because the coefficients in the expressions like $ g(3) = a + g(2) $, $ g(4) = 2a + g(2) $, etc. grow linearly in $ a $.

sentence: But $ g(n) $ is a function from $ \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z} $, and we want to find all such functions satisfying the functional equation.

sentence: Now suppose $ g(n) = 0 $ for all $ n $.

sentence: Then $ f(n) = an $, and this satisfies the functional equation.
